utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. If there is nothing to discuss at the moment, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kralj. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies today. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have the floor, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. God's peace unto this house, and may this day in Court and the final judgement reflect God's will and not mine. And in the manner that will be most beneficial to the souls of all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, good morning. I wish you a pleasant stay among us. We broke off while we were dealing with document D303 yesterday. I would like that document to be displayed again. We have it on our screens. We read three paragraphs yesterday. You know that this is a document of the Main Staff of the VRS, dated 31 August 1994, it was sent to all commands, and the subject line reads: "Order Regarding Movement of Humanitarian Aid Across Lines of Separation." It was signed by General Milovanovic. We saw the signature yesterday. And he said: "You know that the GS of the VRS no longer has any jurisdiction or responsibility concerning approval of entry and movement of teams and convoys of organisations through the territory of Republika Srpska." In the second paragraph, it says: "This approval is now issued --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. Please slow down while reading. The interpreters have a problem. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph two, General Milovanovic says. I quote: "These approvals are now issued by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid and the Ministry of Health, Labour, and Social Welfare. "The Army of Republika Srpska has the obligation to check teams and convoys of humanitarian organisations passing through the territory of Republika Srpska and crossing lines of separation into territory controlled by Muslim and Croatian forces." Fourth paragraph: "The reports that we send to you contain all the information in our possession that we obtain from approvals issued by the afore-mentioned institutions." Mr. Kralj, this document is dated 31 August 1994. Were you familiar with it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What I have just read out to you, was it really implemented in practice the way it's written here, the way it's stated here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was implemented the way it is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were a member of the organ directly in charge of humanitarian convoys moving in the territory of Republika Srpska, can you explain to the Trial Chamber the difference between UNPROFOR convoys and UNHCR convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR convoys were armed convoys. They travelled from their bases to the enclaves and sometimes from a base in Croatia through RS territory to their bases in Sarajevo. They carried personnel and equipment that they needed to carry out their mission. They only supplied UNPROFOR units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to the other question, my answer is that humanitarian convoys carried supplies for the civilian population. That population could be either in RS territory or in the territory controlled by the Muslim Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should recall that this question was put to the witness already yesterday and answered by the witness. You should try to avoid repetitions. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will establish a link now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, tell us if UNPROFOR directly contacted the Main Staff when they wanted to enter VRS controlled territory, or did they contact anybody else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR directly contacted the Main Staff of the VRS through their Pale office, which was in accordance with the agreed procedures. These procedures were agreed by the central joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These other organisations, UNHCR, International Committee of the Red Cross, Doctors Without Frontiers, how did they announce their arrival in RS territory? Please explain, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanitarian organisations, once the co-ordination body of the government was set up, were obliged to submit their requests to that co-ordination body, which was -- which had the exclusive authority for issuing approvals for the movement of humanitarian aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if that co-ordinating body decided how much food could be carried for the enclaves or was somebody else who took such decisions, such as the donors themselves or? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for food, the government co-ordination body often held meetings with representatives of those organisations. It was the donors who decided on the total quantities of food, so it was up to them to decide how much food they would transport to or through the RS, and the co-ordinating body only decided how much could pass in a given period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the role of the VRS, then, with regard to those UNHCR convoys and other humanitarian aid convoys? What were the duties of the VRS in that respect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty of the VRS was to inspect the convoys upon their entry in or exit from VRS controlled territory. They had to guarantee their free passage along the approved routes. They also had to keep a register.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document D307 now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see here a document of the Main Staff of the VRS, dated 16 January 1994. The subject line reads: "Implementation of the Orders by the RS President, Communication." The reference is also to a document in the line below, and it says: "Pursuant to the order of the president of the RS, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, item 3 of order," so-and-so, that's an order of 15 January 1994, "is hereby amended and shall read: "Any dispute issues with representatives of UNPROFOR and military observers shall be resolved exclusively through the corps commands and the Main Staff of the VRS and with international humanitarian organisations through the government co-ordination body for humanitarian aid. "Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Ratko Mladic." Now my question is this: Can you give us some examples of these disputed issues because of which this order was drafted? What kind of issues were those? What happened when convoys passed through and there was a need for communication with them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some UNPROFOR military observers at individual check-points, especially around Sarajevo, were prone not to respect the time and the place of passage. Some vehicles would be announced at one time and would arrive a day earlier. As for humanitarian organisations, some were not aware of the rules, such as Karitas in the Banja Luka region or Merhamet. They tried hard to get approval from the corps to enter RS territory or territory controlled by Muslim Croat forces. In order to alleviate the pressure that arose due to many such issues, this solution was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. The interpreter didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last sentence. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This solution, namely giving authority to the corps command to deal with some minor issues concerning UNPROFOR, reduced the pressure on the VRS Main Staff to deal with petty issues that can successfully be dealt with by corps commands. It was in their mutual interest, especially in the interest of UNPROFOR, because they constantly demanded to be allowed more contacts with lower-ranking units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether the obligation to report or to announce the convoys a day before was a protocol matter or were there other reasons why there was a request to announce the convoy's movement 24 hours in advance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty to announce the convoys 24 hours in advance -- actually, this referred to military observers, for the convoys the period was 48 hours in advance, so in view of the situation in the field it was war, it was a combat zone, and the corps command had to create conditions secure enough for the said convoy to pass safely to its destination at the announced time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P68 in e-court. Actually, P689.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this is coming up, I would like to ask you about the document D307 we have just had on the screen. That was previously in August 2011 MFI'd pending translation. As we could see, the translation is available. Are you tendering it now in full?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence would like to tender it in its entirety. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. It will be received as D307.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at page 2 in the Serbian, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, let's look at article 6. This is a decision on the appointment of a committee for co-operation with the UN and the international humanitarian organisations. It's dated the 14th of March, 1995. Thank you, Aleksandar. I would kindly ask you to look at article 6, please, which states the following: "Permits for the movement of convoys and employees of the UN and humanitarian organisations on the territory of Republika Srpska shall be issued by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian operations, pursuant to committee decisions." Can we now look at article 7, which states: "The committee shall adopt special rules of procedure for issuing permits for the movement of convoys and employees of the UN and humanitarian organisations on the territory of Republika Srpska," end of quote from article 7. My question is: The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, could it change this decision by the committee permitting the movement of convoys in the territory of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a document that can only be amended by the body that issued it. The Main Staff did not have the authority to alter government documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the decision on the appointment of a president, vice-president, and members of the state committee for co-operation with the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations. Thank you. We can see that now on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We're looking at article 1 and 2 which comprise the document. In -- article 2 has nine items. Let's read item 1: "Head of the co-ordinating -- Professor Nikola Koljevic, deputy president of Republika Srpska, is hereby appointed president of the state committee for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations. Maxim Stanisic is hereby appointed deputy president of the state committee for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations." In article 2 that follows, under item 7, it states: The members are listed here. And then in item 7 it states: "Let Colonel Milos Djurdjic -- co-ordinator for the committee's relations with the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska." So do you know, perhaps, what was the role of this co-ordinator of the committee of the Main Staff of the ministry and the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see in article 2, item 7, this references to Colonel Milos Djurdjic. His role in line with the responsibilities of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the corps whose -- through whose territory these convoys would pass was -- first of all, before the passage of the passage of the convoys [Realtime transcript read in error "advise"] was approved, he was to see if the convoy -- if the situation was safe enough for the convoys to pass. And then after that, when the convoy passage was approved by the co-ordination body, it was his job to see that this was safely implemented. They were to inspect the convoys and to keep a record of the goods that were in the convoy that was passing through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D79 in e-court, please, which is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this comes up, one correction for the record, page 9, line 21. The word "advise" should read "convoys." Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We're now looking at Exhibit D79. This is an order from the president of Republika Srpska which states -- actually, the date is the 13th of June, 1995. We're interested in article 2, page 2, point 7. Actually, it's page 2, item 7. And we can see item 7 now which states: "To allow ICRC convoy Zenica-Sarajevo with medical supplies that will be distributed to the Serb and Muslim side along the route that the Supreme HQ of the Army of Republika Srpska assesses as safe. To avoid the route via Ilijas."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: What was the role of the Main Staff in relation to this ICRC convoy? Thank you. What was the role of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the Main Staff was to assess whether the route was safe for passage of said convoy, and it states here "to avoid the route via Ilijas" because that route was not safe. The president already knew that this route was not safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to explain to the Trial Chamber why it wasn't safe, if you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have precise information, but I know that there was some actions underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this case who was in charge of the convoy's safety, the convoy that was announced by the president of Republika Srpska announcing its passage through the territory of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska was in charge of the passage of the convoy or, rather, the Main Staff was through the corps. They were to deal with all matters relating to the safe passage of the convoy through the territory, especially because it was carrying medical supplies that were in short supply everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us if a convoy announced in this way was subject to checks and who carried out these checks at the check-points? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This convoy was subject to the usual control, which implied inspecting the personnel and the equipment that was being carried. They were also obliged to have a list with them of the equipment that they were carrying or which equipment or medicines were approved by the co-ordination body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was already tendered through Witness Nicolai, but only marked for identification because the Witness Nicolai couldn't provide us with any information about this document. Now it will be received as D79. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to look at document 1D935 in e-court, please. Thank you. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, are you able to tell us what kind of document this is? Can you tell what it refers to, who is sending it to whom? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the co-ordinating board for humanitarian aid, dated the 17th of May, 1995. It's signed by Dragan Kekic. The document refers to the UNHCR humanitarian organisation, its Belgrade office, that was supposed to do the following by the 25th of May pursuant to the central plan for equipment supplies. By that date, it was supposed to transport a satellite telex, satellite equipment, computers, adapters. You cannot really see it that well here. Anyway, it was supposed to transport this equipment for the needs of the UNHCR office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read out the first line.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Permission is given for request JUG/PAL/HCR/0241."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was thinking of the note in the text, just below the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in? It's too small. "A weekly plan is hereby approved with the exception of note 3 on page 3."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the co-ordination body presided over by Dragan Kekic forward notes such as this that had to be abided by both those on the convoy and those inspecting it; otherwise, they wouldn't know his notes and remarks were about? In other words, did he forward such documents to both parties involved?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Copies of the same document were sent to both the UNHCR and the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down the page, just under the 26th of May, 1995, it reads: "In addition to the permission, a copy of the approved request and a copy of the bill of lading must be presented. A copy of the bill of lading must be sent to the co-ordinating body through the commission inspector or the border police at the border crossing." Tell us, please, what this instruction was intended for or for whom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an instruction aimed at the UNHCR, stating that they have to be in possession of valid documents. The border people knew of this requirement as well, since the convoy was supposed to go via Karakaj. There was no combat activity there; thus, the civilian police also played an important role at the border crossing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why was it necessary that was person forwarding this document forwarded this to the Main Staff of the VRS as well, by the same token?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the VRS was in charge of control along the demarcation lines facing the enemy. This was for the purposes of control, escort, and an ability to inspect the cargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was authorised to notify the check-point in question about the contents of this document? When someone was to cross the border, who was supposed to notify the border crossing staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the VRS was authorised to inform the border crossing staff of the crossing of a convoy along its lines of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If the co-ordinating body rejected an UNHCR request or a request by some other humanitarian organisations, was the Main Staff informed of it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff was informed regularly about any changes and failure to grant the passage of a convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this another control measure so as to prevent someone who had originally been rejected to try to cross anyway?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If there was an omission or a situation in which someone possessed documents which were not confirmed and accepted, they would still be unable to cross over without the consent of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this admitted, please? Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D935 shall be assigned Exhibit D338. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have 1D01044. We can see that this is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated the 22nd July, 1994. It was sent to the Drina and Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. It was signed by General Milovanovic as we will see on page 2. Could we have that page, please. Thank you. Let us now go back to page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at the first sentence by General Milovanovic: "We are hereby inform you that the co-ordination body of the RS government for humanitarian operations approved the movement," but it seems to be illegible, "of the teams and convoys of humanitarian organisations." And then we have a specification of individual teams and convoys. Towards the bottom of the page it says: "Carry out a check ..." It is the second paragraph from the bottom. "Carry out a check and ensure unhindered movement on the roads approved." My question is this: Did General Milovanovic appropriately use the authority invested in the Main Staff of the VRS when it comes to convoys and humanitarian assistance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I'd like you -- to remind you of the formulation which says: "We are hereby inform you that the co-ordination body approved ..." In other words, the units in question are reminded of the fact that the co-ordinating body is the body which approved the delivery of humanitarian assistance as specified, a followup of which is an instruction to carry out a check and ensure movement on the roads approved. It indicates that the co-ordinating body is the body which made the decision on the convoy to pass through. It was the obligation of the army, or, rather, of the personnel at the check-point to carry out the check and ensure movement on the roads approved. This is different compared to the previous period when the Main Staff was issuing approvals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this the period prior to 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, prior to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have a look at the last paragraph on this page. It reads: "The Drina Corps command must urgently gather, arrange, and submit the overview of humanitarian aid delivered to Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde for the month of July this year. The types and quantities of the following goods must be listed in the overview:" Now we can go to the next page. We have a number of items listed. The document goes on to say the following: "As of 22 July 1994 note all the types and quantities of goods during the checks." In the corps commands which had bodies tasks with the functioning of check-points within the area of responsibility in question, were there registers and log-books kept of the amounts and types of goods that went through the territory of the RS for the needs of the enclaves Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa as mentioned in this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commands had designated personnel who were in charge of keeping lists and records of goods. As of the 22nd of July, 1994, a particular emphasis was placed on that aspect as a result of this order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender the document on the screen, which is 1D01044 so that we can move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D339. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we next have D209. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the screen is a document of the Drina Corps command of the 3rd of May, 1995. It is a breakdown of humanitarian aid to the Muslim enclaves for March and April 1995. There are items from number 1 through to 26, and there is a breakdown for March and April, and as well as per enclave. My question is this: Did you at the Main Staff have access to these records kept by the units in the field within whose areas of responsibility the enclaves were, and did you make use of it? Was it of assistance to you to have such breakdowns and produce summaries?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps pursuant to our request - that is the request made by Colonel Djurdjic - submitted summary breakdowns of what had been transported to enclaves during a given period. Those summaries were like this one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could your organ always give the commander of the Main Staff information about the quantities of food and other items delivered to enclaves for any given month? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our organ was able to provide information at short notice to the commander of the Main Staff, pursuant to his request. That information would be about total quantities of individual kinds of goods during a given month or by convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Colonel Djurdjic, who worked with you and who was chief of the civilian affairs sector, have accurate information about the quantity of articles that arrived in the previous months and was he aware of the needs of the soldiers and civilian population as concerns individual food stuffs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic had the necessary information about the population and the enclave and UNPROFOR presence. He also had information about the quantities of goods delivered to the individual enclaves during any given period. The information was accurate or, rather, accurately collected, especially after that order that we saw, I think it was dated 22 July 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need to take you back to -- I am addressing this question to the witness. I want to take you back to page 17 of today's transcript, starting with line 18. I am referring specifically to the question by General Tolimir where he said: "Did you at the Main Staff [Realtime transcript read in error "ministry"] have access to these records kept by the units in the field within whose areas of responsibility the enclaves were, and did you make use of it?" I don't think in your answer you answered those questions. Do you think you can answer those questions for me, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this part about the "ministry" because I was at the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the followup question was: "Was it of assistance to you to have such breakdowns ...?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was of great assistance to have such breakdowns. It enabled us to inform the commander how much was delivered to the individual enclaves when he demanded such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a followup question to you. Perhaps you misunderstood or it was a translation issue, the question of Mr. Tolimir repeated by my colleague Judge Nyambe. There was no reference to a ministry. The question was: "Did you at the Main Staff have access to these records kept by the units in the field?" There was only a reference to the Main Staff. Could you now answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to requests by Colonel Djurdjic, the units regularly submitted such reports. Usually that would be a summary monthly report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, did Colonel Djurdjic take care that everything was done in accordance with the relevant standards and did he inform the Chief of Staff of anything being or not being in accordance with the standards? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic had access to the applicable standards, and if he noticed that something deviated from the standards he would point that out to the commander or whoever had the duty to take the relevant decision. He would inform that person that a quantity was either normal or otherwise and thus usable for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Main Staff in case of abnormal or great quantities able to conclude that what was actually being done was the setting up of war reserves by either UNPROFOR or humanitarian organisations? Was the Main Staffs able to draw such a conclusion based on the breakdowns we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible to conclude that reserves were being formed based on monitoring the quantities of goods entering the enclaves. Those goods could either be -- could either have been transported there by UNPROFOR or by other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 65 ter 1787. Thank you. Thank you. Please enlarge because the witness has repeatedly requested the enlargement of the document because the letters are small.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document of the Main Staff dated 7 March, 1995. It says, I quote: "We would like to inform you that we approve the authorisation kot number 361," and there is a number of abbreviations and so on. Do you know what these abbreviations stand for and what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, can you read that or should it be zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just read about half, a little more. It would be good if it could be enlarged, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is difficult to enlarge it. Yes, exactly. That --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's better legible now. The first thing I notice is that this is an open text that was sent to the command of military post number 7111 and military post number 7598. These are the civilian designations of military post numbers that were used for the delivery of mail; that is, the communication channel was not a protected military channel. And then it says: "We would like to inform you that we approve the authorisation kot for hp ..." This is the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid of the Republika Srpska. And then a reference is made to document 361-MKCK which stands for International Committee of the Red Cross which was filed at Pale under number 95/265/n. It refers to the delivery of medical material from Pale to Zepa. Departure on 8 March and return on the same day along the route Pale-Podromanija-Rogatica-Zepa and back along the same route. The team consists of the persons mentioned here: Miljana Jelic, ID 2328 - ID standing for identity document - she had that document as a member of that humanitarian aid organisation. The second person mentioned is Danijela Krneta, whose ID number is 2322. And then there are the vehicles yg 019 Geneva. The vehicle number is 5244. The second vehicle is yg 140 Geneva 5294. These are the license plate numbers on the vehicles of the ICRC. Content: ICRC mail such as letters and whatever. Then personnel belongings and medical material, as listed in the document carried by the team leader. I would like to say that the International Committee of the Red Cross is one of the international organisations -- can you hear me? One of the organisations which was impartial in this process and never created problems when it comes to following procedures. On this occasion, they were given approval to carry a list showing the quantity of goods they were carrying. And based on that list, an inspection was made and report was drafted. It also goes on to say: "Check and enable free passage on the approved routes." Can we scroll down?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This will do for the moment. Let's keep it this way because I want to ask you about the first line of this cable. Thank you. The first sentence of this cable reads: "We would like to inform you that we" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Approve of the authorisation," it should be. Interpreter's remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why this language, "inform you that we approve of"? For whom is this meant?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This word, "approve," well it wasn't really necessary. It would have been enough to say, We inform you that the co-ordination body approved this or that. But the operatives added this word because they were wont to use such phrases, but this document could have -- could have been drafted without this word, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And this, "We would like to inform you that we approve ...," does that refer to -- actually, who does that refer to? Thank you. To whom is this sent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is sent to the check-point, to the military post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you know, did the Main Staff review at any point whether it should give its approval or not to the decision of the co-ordinating board?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff did take part in the process before the co-ordinating body reached its decision. If it received the body's decision, then it was supposed to implement it, not to give its approval if the decision had already been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us how the Main Staff knew what some humanitarian organisation was requesting and how did it know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff would receive information or the request from the co-ordinating body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And the co-ordinator of the co-ordinating body of the Main Staff, did they have any influence or effect on that decision? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The co-ordinator had any influence only in the area of control and to indicate whether certain routes were safe for passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you're talking about security, your department for civilian affairs, did it have information as to how and in what way the inhabitants acted towards the convoys that were passing through the territory of Republika Srpska or the territory which was controlled by the enemy? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were revolts by the inhabitants in some areas opposing the passage of the humanitarian aid convoys through the territory under the control of the Muslim Croat forces or to the territory under the control of the Muslim Croat forces, especially in the direction of Tesanj towards Travnik and also in the direction of Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us why the inhabitants demonstrated this kind of attitude towards the convoys that were supplying the Muslim Croat federation territory through the territory of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat actions with soldiers who were from the families at the line of separation were killed, wounded, from certain places in the territory of the Army of Republika Srpska. There were incursions by groups or small groups that were carrying out different massacres. This is the first thing. The second thing is during a certain period there was no aid from those organisations distributed to the population of Republika Srpska. So they were dissatisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you talking about the period when there were sanctions imposed by the United Nations and by humanitarian organisations imposed by countries that were opposed, and they were imposed on Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this does refer to that period. I stress that Serbia also had imposed sanctions, whereby the humanitarian situation in Republika Srpska was even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber how the Main Staff dealt with this resistance by the inhabitants since they were those that they were not in friendly relations with but they were receiving humanitarian assistance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff took all measures, including escorts of the convoys, up to the line of confrontation, and then in some cases also the civilian police participated where this was deemed necessary, such as was the case in the 1st Krajina Corps where the convoys moved along a longer route from Gradiska through Banja Luka, Jajce and towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we must have our first break now and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would just like to give you an explanation. I am obliged to tell Mr. Vanderpuye that today he will be able to begin his cross-examination of this witness. This is something that I promised yesterday. We are going to finish in the next session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this information. It is appreciated. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we continue with the examination of the witness, I would just shortly raise one matter. The parties will be aware of the fact that the Defence in the Perisic case urgently requested, yesterday afternoon, access to confidential material in our case. We all realise that in their case it is a very urgent matter. Therefore, I would kindly ask the parties if they are in a position to respond to that orally tomorrow morning and to give us their position on this requested so that we can address that, we, as a Chamber, address this matter by filing as soon as possible. Would that be possible for both parties to give oral submissions tomorrow morning at the outset of the hearing tomorrow morning? Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Of course, we'll be prepared to address the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence is also prepared. We can even say now that we are in agreement that everything that was requested can be disclosed, so you can consider that we have stated our opinion now instead of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. In this case, I would ask the Prosecution if they are in a position to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First I want to continue my sentence. I just gave you the opportunity to consult. I wanted to ask if you are in a position to make an oral submission already today, either now or at the end of today's hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We may be able to do it at the end of the hearing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is very helpful. So if we have resolved this problem, then we should continue the examination of the witness. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor again. Just a moment, Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to go back to something that was said just before the break, page 23, line 23 of today's transcript. We can see and read in English the following sentence that: "... the co-ordinator of the co-ordinating body of the Main Staff ..." That's what you said. So I just wanted to get a clarification. Are you saying that within the co-ordination commission, which belonged to the government, there was a representative of the Main Staff and that person also had the title of a co-ordinator? Is that what you wanted to say or is there a mistake in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, you can see that -- the relevant part on the screen now, page 23, line 23. Perhaps the Court Usher can assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a co-ordinator representing the Main Staff for co-operation with the co-ordinating body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So what you are telling us is that this is not a VRS co-ordination commission, but it's rather the co-ordinator who is the representative of the Main Staff within the co-ordination commission; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, I have another question I would like to put to you. Just before the break, and this is on page 24, lines 19 and 20, you said the following, and it will appear to the screen in a moment. You said, and I quote: "There were incursions by groups or small groups that were carrying out different massacres." Could you give us some more details about what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in the territory of Srebrenica going towards or directed at Kravica with Muslim groups making incursions into the territory, although the territory was already under the control of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "different massacres"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Individual killings, either of civilians or members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To understand your statement in full, is it correct that you are saying Muslim groups encircled Serb groups and comitted massacres? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is it. There were sudden attacks of small groups which could attack and pull-out unhindered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In which time-period did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, thank you for your patience. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During the last session we discussed the issue of humanitarian organisations and problems which arose when they crossed RS territory to reach federation territory which was under Muslim BH Army control, and they provided supplies to them. Can you tell us something more about the problems you have just discussed with us, which occurred between May and late June 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were continued attacks on the units and civilians which came from the territory of Srebrenica. Srebrenica at the time was under UNPROFOR control. There were several such instances, including groups, individuals, reconnaissance activities, and killings of both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly tell us whether this situation in which the groups attacked civilians and soldiers in RS territory and in the protected areas had an impact on the overall situation with the convoys which supplied them and UNPROFOR which protected them before they returned to the territory which was controlled by their forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the basic reason why the population in those areas objected to both UNPROFOR and the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are on this topic, tell us if you know whether there were such attacks on the Main Staff, on the roads, and villages? Were any villages torched by the sabotage groups which came from the territory of the Muslim Croat federation or from Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the accused be asked to turn the microphone towards him, not away from him? We have trouble hearing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, did you hear the interpreter's note? Please turn the microphone -- turn the microphones toward your head so that the interpreter's can hear you better.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The accused, please. Not the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I thought it was an address to Mr. Kralj. It was an address to you, Mr. Tolimir. Yes, thank you. Mr. Kralj, now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were attacks on the Main Staff of the VRS which were repelled successfully. There were attacks on the village as well. The attack on the Main Staff of the VRS came from the direction of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Tell us, please, whether there were problems with convoy movements across RS territory during the bombing campaign in May 1995 and later? And I have in mind the bombing campaign against the RS.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, there were no problems. During the bombing, everyone stopped moving about, whether such movements had been announced, planned or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber who was it that halted all convoy movement in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was halted by those who sent the convoys. It was not the co-ordinating body but the UNHCR and other organisations. They simply did not see their plans through; although, they did not even notify us that they would give up on their plans in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Between May and July 1995 when the attack on Srebrenica occurred, was it a frequent occurrence or was it only specific to May 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a common occurrence and it did not only take place in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it also take place during the bombing of the RS by NATO, when different facilities were bombed in RS territory in August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no convoys arriving during August and September. And especially so when there were immediate air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have problems communicating because the relay stations and other facilities were destroyed by bombing, and how did you co-ordinate your work with the co-ordinating body and UNPROFOR in terms of being able to relay messages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to bombardment and the fact that the relay stations were destroyed, there were no telephone lines. There were no other electronic means to communicate, so we established courier connections. In other words, we sent a vehicle with a courier to transport mail on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj, for your answers. Can you tell us whether your department for co-operation and civilian affairs, irrespective of the bombing and other problems, always treated UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations in the same way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were professional. It was our task to communicate with them, irrespective of what was going on. Nothing changed in our relationship towards them, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you feel any change the way these international bodies and organisations saw the VRS and RS population in terms of how they continued providing humanitarian assistance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could clearly see that they were afraid. Later on, when things got back to normal, that co-operation improved again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what period exactly it is? What month and year?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following August and September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kralj, in the introductory part yesterday you said that you attended some talks in Vienna, and during your testimony you mentioned Vienna, Tolimir, and Talic. Let us try and clear it up. Can you tell us what the talks in Vienna were about, the ones you and Tolimir participated in and what were the activities of General Talic in Vienna before he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was a member of a negotiating team alongside General Tolimir when the implementation of Annex 1D of the Dayton Accords was concerned, in particular Articles II and IV. Article II had to do with confidence building measures between the VRS and BH Army and the Federation and the RS. It also had to do with the quantities and types of weapons and control, mutual control, of those assets that the two armed forces were entitled to under the article. Article IV included some other participants in the talks so as to include Croatia and the then-FRY. The talks took place under OSCE auspices. That's the first part. The second part regarding General Talic. Together with him, I took part in a number of working meetings at a higher level, including army commanders in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as ministers of defence. We visited Brussels, London, and the last stop was Vienna when we talked to the OSCE again. I wasn't present then, as that was the occasion when General Talic was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Can you tell the Chamber the month and year of the Vienna talks that you participated in with General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in late 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was an agreement signed as a result of those talks between the warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina and a number of different former Yugoslav republics?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those meetings resulted in the signing of an agreement, which was finalised by an agreement on the reduction of weapons assets in -- which in its final stage include Croatia and the FRY as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you take part in the implementation of the signed agreements, and can you tell us when the implementation activities pertaining to the agreements were undertaken?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first agreement we signed was the one under Article II. Once it was signed, it began being implemented right away. Once the Article IV agreement was signed and once the arms verification centre was established, I acted as the leader of escort team on the RS side. We received Federation inspections as well as inspections from Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Under certain procedure which was arranged with the OSCE and the parties in Vienna, our inspections, in turn, were received by the armed forces of Croatia, the FRY, Bosnia and Herzegovina, although it did not have its single armed force but they, too, wanted to be a side to the agreement. In Vienna all information was exchanged about the weapons of each of the sides in keeping with the agreement. I was often present at such occasions with General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, now, did the activities to implement the disarmament agreement and arms control continue throughout 1996 in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1996 was a year of -- marked by activities under these agreements, especially activities aimed at the reduction of the quantity of weapons. There were more weapons than envisaged by the agreement. In the agreement there were specific limits with regard to calibre, the number of pieces, and so on, that each party was entitled to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you and I, as RS negotiators, report regularly on everything that we comitted to on behalf of the RS with regard to the reduction of the quantity of weapons? Did we report on that regularly to both military and civilian authorities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a very topical matter during that period. After any action taken by the commission in Vienna, a report was drafted that was sent to both the Main Staff and the civilian authorities of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How much of your time did that take? I mean the preparations for the implementation of the agreement within the RS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took a lot of our time. There was a need to establish a separate group within the department to deal with these matters, such as the preparation of information, the forwarding of information about weapons, the collecting, and later a separate body had to be established for these inspections and for receiving inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj, for coming to this Tribunal to testify about past events. Thank you for replies you gave. The Defence has no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, Mr. President. We can now give the Prosecution the opportunity to examine the witness. I would just kindly ask for an opportunity to see the witness after this examination later on in the Detention Unit, because the witness has expressed such a wish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. There are two matters: One is that there is still one document on the screen. This is 65 ter 1787. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you for reminding us, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D340. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the other matter, you asked for the opportunity to meet Witness Kralj. This will be decided at a later stage, and we will come back to that. Now it's the turn for the Prosecution for their cross-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. Kralj. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of the Prosecution I am going to put some questions to you in respect of your direct examination which has just been completed by General Tolimir. If I ask you anything that's unclear, let me know, and I will try to rephrase it or state it in a way that we can better understand one another. And if there is anything you would like me to repeat, also let me know, and I will do the same. Let me just start by asking you a couple of questions. General Tolimir just mentioned that you had expressed a desire to see him following your testimony here today. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expressed the desire to visit him at the Detention Unit, and I submitted the documents required for that. I did that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw General Tolimir before you had been testifying here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just so there is no misunderstanding, as far as I know both Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Kralj submitted the required documents for a visit tomorrow rather than today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is only to be considered for a time after your testimony. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said that the last time you saw General Tolimir was some 15 years ago. Have you been in contact with members of his Defence before testifying here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first contact with Aleksandar was a telephone conversation in which he asked me if I would be willing to testify in this trial. That was some 20 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now you've indicated your first contact. How many contacts did you have with, when you say Aleksandar, I assume you mean Mr. Gajic, before testifying in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I heard that it would be about a subject matter with which I am familiar, I agreed. Upon arriving to The Hague on the 21st, I had consultations with him. That was on a Saturday and Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say you had consultations with him, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman acquainted me with the procedures applied by this Tribunal and with the parts of the indictment - he didn't go into details, however - and he said what the hearing would be about. I replied that I had previously testified in General Miletic's trial. I understood that the subject matter to be dealt with was the work of the civilian affairs department and that the most important point would be the prevention of the passage of humanitarian aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you discussed the basic subject matter of your testimony with Mr. Gajic; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you also informed Mr. Gajic that you had testified in the case in the Defence of General Miletic back in 2008 December; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him that I had testified, but I didn't go into the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review your testimony in that case, that is the case of Prosecutor versus Popovic et al., your testimony from 3 through 5 December 2008 in the Defence of Radivoje Miletic, one of the accused in that case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you reviewed that testimony since you testified in 2008?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you confirm to this Trial Chamber that that testimony that you gave was as truthful and accurate as it could have been in the circumstances at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The testimony was truthful, given the circumstances at the time. I believe I would give the same testimony even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's helpful to know. General Tolimir asked you a lot of questions about the facts and circumstances surrounding the events in 1995 and, indeed, periods beyond and preceding that, and you seem to have a pretty good recollection of some of that material. Let me ask you, Mr. Kralj, can you tell the Trial Chamber when it was that you first heard that thousands of Muslim men from Srebrenica had been murdered in July 1995 by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was published in the media, the BH Federation media. I saw it on television. And I saw it only a few days after the alleged events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When would that be? The end of July? Beginning of August? Can you give us some indication.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you a couple of questions about your background. Now, you were assigned to the VRS Main Staff I think you indicated on the 3rd of November, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You came there from the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While you were in the Krajina Corps, you performed the functions of a liaison officer with international organisations and UNPROFOR and the like; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the civilian affairs sector of the corps and that was their duty. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you went to the Main Staff, you worked there as an officer in the sector for civilian affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an officer and an interpreter. Actually, that was my main duty, to interpret into and from English. And I was assigned to the civilian affairs sector, headed by Colonel Djurdjic, to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic headed up the civilian affairs sector. You were one of the members of that sector. Did you work with Colonel Pandzic as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also collaborated with Colonel Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Besides the three of you, who else worked in that sector?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. Colonel Pandzic did not belong to that sector. He was a chief of aviation. We only collaborated with him concerning UNPROFOR helicopter sorties toward protected zones, so he did not belong to that sector. He was chief of aviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Who else worked in the sector?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came there, there were just Colonel Djurdjic and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was that the case throughout your tenure in that sector, or did that change?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sector was later reinforced with personnel in the framework of the implementation of Articles 4 and 2 of the agreement that we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you collaborated with Colonel Pandzic who was a member of the airforce. Who else did you collaborate with?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was at the disposal of all those who submitted a request to Colonel Djurdjic for an interpreter at meetings. However, the priorities were clearly defined. The commander had the highest priority and then it went further down along the chain of command. That applied in the case of simultaneous meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your sector liaised with international organisations; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And other international organisations and NGOs; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also had substantive responsibilities beyond being an interpreter; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that sector to which I was assigned to work, my duty was to get acquainted with all documents and work procedures to be able to do administrative work during the absence of Colonel Djurdjic, administrative work that had to do with the functioning of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, that administrative work had to do with, for example, inspecting check-points - right? - in relation to the movement of convoy material?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "Yes, in a way." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We followed the problems that occurred at the check-points and issued relevant guidelines or instructions in order to improve things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said yesterday that your role was to inspect the check-point, draw up a short report as to whether the instructions were abided by, that you were authorised to instruct personnel on how to communicate with convoy members in an appropriate way. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. That was my role in the 1st Krajina Corps where I was liaison officer, and I was present both in the control of check-points and I was involved in escorting convoys through RS territory but that was there. That was not the case when I was with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see. So when you were with the Main Staff, you didn't engage whatsoever in the administration of check-points throughout, let's say, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you had no idea how those convoys were actually being administered; is that right? At the check-points, I should add.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have an idea how they were supposed to do it and I had an idea of how they did it, but that was not my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you train members of the convoys of -- of check-points?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please specify as to when and where?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were in the Main Staff, did you participate in training members of these convoy inspection units?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You only did that in the Krajina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did that initially during the time when a particular check-point was being set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you were in the Krajina Corps, you also made sure the check-points were regularly reporting to the disposition of convoys - right? - up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the duty of the unit manning the check-point. They had means of communication, and in their combat report there was an item about the situation in the territory which included the passage of convoys, be it humanitarian or UNPROFOR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand whose duty it was. My question is: Did you make sure that that duty was carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was part of my job. I was maintaining records of all the reports that would reach the command. The command was some 50 kilometres away from the check-point, so I wasn't at the check-point all the time. The reports would come to the command, to the sector for civilian affairs, to Colonel Vujnovic and then he would issue assignments. And then other than this job, I also had the job of an interpreter which was quite intensive work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While you were at the Main Staff, who undertook those responsibilities with respect to the personnel in the administration of check-points regarding convoys from -- either from UNPROFOR or humanitarian aid sources?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was Colonel Djurdjic's main work and his main task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the reports that were generated in respect of the movement of these convoys at the various check-points, those reports were sent up to the Main Staff, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And those reports, when they were sent to the Main Staff, were reviewed by officers of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did anybody review these reports that came from the check-points to the Main Staff, either directly or indirectly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the reports -- actually, I would like to ask you to clarify a little bit. I said that the report on the work and the passage at the check-point from the unit where the check-point was, was part of the combat report, it was a paragraph in it, and it would arrive to the duty officer. Those combat reports were sent to the commander for his review. Colonel Djurdjic would read what was necessary from those reports, and if there was something of interest for him, good or bad, he would note that down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So Colonel Djurdjic would review these reports, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer would review them and the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Djurdjic would read what was necessary from those reports; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The reports were addressed to the commander - right? - as part of a combat report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They would be reviewed by the commander, or at least they were intended to be reviewed by the commander; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander would usually review all the reports, all the combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about the deputy commander, General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic also reviewed the reports. However, in practice it turned out that they were at the command post very rarely at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about the assistant commanders?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant commanders dealt with issues from their line of work from the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir was assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs. So he was dealing with issues that he was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He was a member of the joint commission that you testified about, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You identified his initials and signature on documents relating to the disposition of convoys; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He submitted proposals to the commander as to what to do with these convoy requests from UNPROFOR in the documents you've identified; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He submitted proposals. He would give proposals, if that was what was asked of him, but he wasn't obliged to have an overview of all the convoys. Milos also could have submitted that to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Milos did, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were any disputed issues, if he noticed any, before giving it to the commander, he could consult with General Tolimir. These could be matters from the domain of the joint military commission, and this is what he did regularly whenever he had the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I want to know from you, Mr. Kralj, is whether or not General Tolimir in his capacity or in his -- given his involvement in convoy issues reviewed reports containing the disposition of those convoys that were sent to the Main Staff? And I don't want you to guess. If you know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. I am not guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What's your answer, then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurdjic would review the report. If he thought that something was not clear which had to be submitted for the commander's signature or placed in his documentation, if he had the opportunity he could consult General Tolimir, but he was not obliged nor was the procedure such that he had to take a document first for General Tolimir's review and then to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, my question is pretty straight forward. You said that there were documents concerning the convoys and the disposition of the convoys that were sent to the Main Staff and they were contained in a combat report. These were reviewed by the commander or deputy commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were reports where the activities of the check-point were noted and they were part of the combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
